opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's not wrong, exactly. There is a diffusion module at the end of AlphaFold 3, and it's what actually produces the atomic coordinates. But if you just say "it's a diffusion model," people picture something like an image generator where the denoising network is doing all the heavy lifting, and that's really not where most of the work happens.

The bulk of the computation, and I'd argue most of the scientific understanding, lives in the trunk. That's the part that takes in the sequences, the multiple sequence alignment information, any templates, and builds up a very rich representation of the pairwise relationships between residues and atoms. In AlphaFold 3 that's the Pairformer, which descends quite directly from the Evoformer in AlphaFold 2. By the time you reach the diffusion module, the network has largely decided what the structure is. It has worked out which parts contact which, what the geometry roughly looks like. The diffusion module is conditioned on that representation and turns it into precise 3D coordinates.

So I sometimes describe the diffusion part as the "rendering" stage. It's very important, and it bought us real things. We could drop a lot of the hand-crafted, protein-specific machinery from AlphaFold 2, like the frames and the torsion-angle parameterization and the stereochemical violation losses. That made it much easier to handle ligands, nucleic acids, modified residues, and arbitrary chemistry in a uniform way. And because it's generative, you can sample multiple plausible structures. But it isn't where the model reasons about evolution or physics. That's the trunk.

There's also a subtlety the label hides. Generative models will happily produce something plausible-looking even where the model doesn't know the answer. In AlphaFold 2, disordered regions came out as these obvious spaghetti ribbons, which was honest. A pure diffusion model can hallucinate compact, structured-looking regions that aren't really there. We had to deal with that deliberately, partly by training on AlphaFold 2 predictions, a sort of cross-distillation, so the model learned to output that extended, low-confidence appearance for disordered regions. And the confidence heads, pLDDT, PAE and so on, remain essential, because you need the model to tell you when to trust a sample.

So if you call it a diffusion model, you capture the output mechanism and miss most of what makes it work: the representation learning in the trunk, the use of evolutionary information, the training data and distillation choices, and the confidence estimation. Diffusion is the last mile, not the whole road.

r002.rationale: It describes the trunk as establishing contacts and rough geometry, then says diffusion uses that representation to produce precise 3D coordinates.

r003.rationale: It does not describe AlphaFold 2’s structural solution order or a reversal in when large-scale structure is resolved.

r004.rationale: It argues that calling AlphaFold 3 a diffusion model misses much of how it works, but does not connect architectural labels to explaining advances in model performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the diffusion part is real, but it's the least interesting part of the system, honestly. If you look at AlphaFold 3, the diffusion module is where the atomic coordinates actually get generated. It takes noised coordinates and learns to denoise them, and that's a nice way to handle the fact that we're now dealing with arbitrary molecules, not just protein chains. We don't have to hand-build a frame representation for every ligand and nucleic acid and modification. We just put atoms in space and let the network clean them up.

But almost everything that makes the model work happens before that. The bulk of the compute, the bulk of the parameters, is in the trunk, the pairformer. That's where the model is reasoning about which residues are close to which, what the evolutionary signal is telling you, how the interfaces are forming. By the time you get to the diffusion module, the hard problem of figuring out the structure has essentially been solved in this abstract pairwise representation. The diffusion module is reading that off and turning it into coordinates. It's conditioned so heavily on the trunk that calling the whole thing a diffusion model is a bit like describing a car by its wheels.

And you can see this in the behavior. If you run the diffusion sampler with a trunk that hasn't converged, you get garbage. If you have a good trunk, you get good structures even with relatively few sampling steps. The generative process isn't exploring the space of structures the way an image diffusion model explores the space of images. It's mostly a decoder with a bit of stochasticity, which helps with things like the sidechain packing and with handling genuinely ambiguous regions.

I'd also say the framing matters for what people take away. Diffusion models in the public imagination are about generating diverse plausible samples. That's not what we want. We want the right answer, and we want the model to tell us when it doesn't know. So the diffusion module is really a tool for geometry, and the understanding, the biology if you like, lives elsewhere in the network.

r002.rationale: It describes the diffusion module as turning the trunk’s informative pairwise representation into coordinates and refining geometric details such as sidechain packing.

r003.rationale: It does not compare AlphaFold 2 and AlphaFold 3 or describe a reversal in when large-scale structure is resolved.

r004.rationale: It argues that calling AlphaFold 3 a diffusion model is incomplete, but does not claim that architectural labels fail to explain advances in model performance.

astra-6.text:
Well, calling it a diffusion model tells you something about how we generate the coordinates, but it doesn’t tell you where the understanding of the molecular system comes from. You could build a diffusion model that produces very plausible-looking molecular structures and still gets the interactions completely wrong.

A lot of the work happens in the network that reasons about the inputs and builds up representations of the relationships between atoms and residues. The diffusion module uses that information to turn noisy coordinates into a structure. Those two pieces have to work together: you need to work out what constraints the structure should satisfy, and then you need to realize those constraints in three dimensions.

So diffusion is an important part of the answer, but it’s not a complete explanation of the capability. It describes the mechanism for producing a structure more than it explains how the system knows which structure to produce.

r002.rationale: It describes the network as supplying information about structural constraints and diffusion as turning noisy coordinates into a structure that realizes those constraints in 3D.

r003.rationale: It does not compare when large-scale structure is resolved in AlphaFold 2 versus AlphaFold 3.

r004.rationale: It says the diffusion label alone does not explain AlphaFold 3’s capability, but does not connect architectural labels to advances in model performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “diffusion model” describes an important part of how we generate the structure, but it doesn’t really explain where the ability to predict that structure comes from. You can say that we start with noisy coordinates and progressively denoise them, but that leaves a huge question: how does the network know what to denoise them toward?

A lot of the work is in building up representations of the molecules and their relationships—reasoning about which parts interact and what those interactions imply about the structure. The diffusion component uses that information to produce coordinates. So if you focus entirely on diffusion, you miss much of the machinery that makes the predictions useful.

It’s a bit like describing a language model by saying it predicts the next token. That tells you something important about the formulation, but it doesn’t, by itself, explain the capabilities of the system.

r001.rationale: The response says the network’s molecular representations inform the diffusion component, but does not state that the overall structure is largely determined by the preceding network together with the first diffusion pass.

r002.rationale: It says diffusion uses molecular information to produce coordinates, but does not clearly characterize diffusion as realizing geometric details within already informative structural constraints.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare when AlphaFold 2 and AlphaFold 3 resolve large-scale structure.

r004.rationale: It argues that calling the system a diffusion model describes an important part of its formulation but does not explain where its predictive ability or useful capabilities come from.
